43.title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
43.hook: two people who waited a long time recognize the baby in the temple
43.howItsDone: Many churches keep the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, often called Candlemas, when candles are blessed. Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, is sung or said at the close of the day in Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds: the night shift heard the news first, and Mary kept it all.

The temple courts are loud. Pilgrims, priests, animals, coins changing hands. Forty days after a birth, the law of Moses asked a mother to come to the temple, and a firstborn son was presented to God. Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to Jerusalem, with the offering the law allowed for families who couldn't afford a lamb: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. Nobody is watching a young couple from Galilee with a baby and two birds. Nobody except two people: a widow of great age, and a man who has been waiting a long time. Both of them know what they're looking at.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OLD.` → `TWO BIRDS, NOT A LAMB.` → `TWO PEOPLE, WAITING.`

segments.voice: Luke introduces Simeon: "the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." Waiting for the comfort of his people. Luke says the Spirit had shown him he would not die before he saw the one God promised. That day he's led into the temple, takes the baby in his arms, and says: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." He calls the child a light for the nations and the glory of Israel. In Latin those first words are Nunc dimittis, and Simeon's song has been sung at the end of the day for many centuries: at evening prayer by Anglicans, at night prayer by Catholics, at vespers by Orthodox Christians. Then he turns to Mary with a harder word: a sword will pierce her own soul too. And then Anna. A prophetess, Luke says, very old, married seven years and then a widow, "which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Luke gives a number, eighty-four, and nobody is sure if it's her age or her years as a widow. She comes up that same hour, gives thanks, and starts telling everyone who is waiting too. Notice who recognizes the child. Not the powerful. A man who came when the Spirit led him, and a widow who kept showing up. Luke never gives Simeon's age; painters make him old because he speaks of departing in peace. In Luke's telling, waiting isn't sitting still. It's coming back, day after day, looking.
screen: `JUST AND DEVOUT, WAITING.` · `NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART.` · `A SWORD FOR MARY'S SOUL.` · `ANNA, NIGHT AND DAY.` · then, large: `MINE EYES HAVE SEEN THY SALVATION.`

segments.voice: Think of someone older who has waited a long time for something, a letter, a recovery, a call from a child: what did the waiting cost them, and what did it teach them? If you pray, hold them before God; if you don't, honor them quietly in your mind.
Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you let go: the first words of Simeon's song, after he held the infant Jesus.
Your line: waiting is not wasted. Next, stargazers from the east, and the road toward Galilee.

44.title: The magi (Matthew 2:1–12)
44.hook: stargazers from the east follow a light and kneel before a toddler
44.howItsDone: Western churches celebrate the magi at Epiphany on January 6, and in many countries children mark it with processions, sweets or chalked blessings over doorways. In Orthodox churches January 6 centers on the baptism of Jesus, and the magi are remembered at Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon and Anna and the Nunc dimittis: two people who had waited, and knew the child when he came. Waiting is not wasted. Today a new stretch of the road begins, the road through Galilee.

Jerusalem, a king's court, and visitors nobody expected. Matthew says they came from the east: men who read the night sky for meaning. Far away they saw something they couldn't ignore, and they set out. Matthew doesn't say how long the road was, or how many walked it. Only that they came, and that in the capital they asked a dangerous question out loud: "Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him." The king on the throne is Herod.
screen: `A KING'S COURT, AND VISITORS.` → `A STAR IN THE EAST.` → `WHERE IS HE THAT IS BORN KING?`

segments.voice: Matthew calls them magoi, and never says how many. Three is a later guess, from the three gifts. He never calls them kings either; that came later, from psalms about kings bringing gifts. The names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar come from later legend. Magoi meant something like wise men or astrologers: learned stargazers, perhaps from Persia or Babylon, though Matthew says only the east, and outsiders to Israel's faith. Herod is troubled, Matthew says, and all Jerusalem with him. The chief priests and scribes look it up: the prophet Micah points to Bethlehem. Herod sends the visitors on and asks them to come back and tell him where the child is, so he can worship too. He doesn't mean it. The star goes before them, and when it stops, "they rejoiced with exceeding great joy." Matthew piles up the words. They find the child with Mary his mother, in a house, and they kneel. Then they open their treasures: "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." An old Christian reading takes them as gold for a king, incense for God, myrrh for a death to come. Then, warned in a dream, they go home another way. Notice: the first people in Matthew's Gospel to worship Jesus are foreigners, following the light they had, a star, not a scripture. Western churches remember them at Epiphany, the feast of the light shown to the nations.

segments.voice: Ask what has been pulling at your attention lately: not a duty but a curiosity, a question you keep coming back to, a book you keep meaning to open, a person you'd like to know better, a place you keep wondering about. Don't judge whether it's important; the magi followed a light in the sky, so just find yours and look at it for a while. If you pray, you can ask where it leads.
The magi. Stargazers from the east, no number given, who followed a light and knelt before a child. Our word magic comes from the same root.
Your line: follow the star you have. Tomorrow, the road turns dark. See you then.

45.title: The flight into Egypt (Matthew 2:13–23)
45.hook: the holy family become refugees, fleeing a king's violence by night
45.howItsDone: Many churches remember the flight into Egypt in the days after Christmas, along with the Holy Innocents, and many Christian charities point to this story in their work with refugees. Coptic Christians celebrate the Holy Family's arrival in Egypt each year and visit places tradition links to their journey.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the magi: stargazers who followed a light, knelt before a child, and went home another way. Follow the star you have.

A family packs in the dark. No time for goodbyes. Whatever fits in their arms, and a child who doesn't understand why he's been woken. They leave before sunrise, heading for a border, because staying means someone they love may be killed. That happens somewhere in the world tonight. In Matthew's Gospel it happens to Mary, Joseph and the child. The magi have gone home another way, and Herod, the king who asked where the child was, has worked out that he's been tricked. And Joseph has another dream.
screen: `PACKING IN THE DARK.` → `HEROD HAS BEEN TRICKED.` → `JOSEPH DREAMS AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The angel's words are urgent: "Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him." Joseph does it that same night. He never speaks a single word in the Gospels. He just gets up and goes. Then comes the darkest scene in the Christmas story. Herod, furious, orders every boy of two and under in and around Bethlehem to be killed. Matthew is the only source for this; no other writer of the time mentions it, though Herod was known to be ruthless, even with his own sons. Matthew quotes the prophet Jeremiah: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The story doesn't hurry past the grief. Churches still keep a day for these children, the Holy Innocents, in the days after Christmas. And Egypt, the old land of slavery in the Exodus story, is now the place of safety. Matthew quotes another prophet, Hosea: "Out of Egypt have I called my son." Israel's story, lived again in one child. Coptic Christians in Egypt still trace the places they say the family stayed, and celebrate its arrival every year. Then Herod dies, Joseph dreams again, and they come home, not to Bethlehem but to a small town in Galilee called Nazareth. Before he preached, before he healed, before anyone knew his name, Jesus was a child carried across a border by night.

segments.voice: Think of one family that has had to leave home, someone you know, someone you saw in the news, or your own family a generation or two back, and picture them clearly: the packing, the road, the first night somewhere strange. If you pray, pray for them by name, or for the family whose name you'll never know; if you don't, just keep them in mind with care.
Holy Innocents. The name churches still use for the children Herod had killed in and around Bethlehem, grieved in Matthew's Gospel and remembered every year after Christmas.

46.title: The boy in the temple (Luke 2:41–52)
46.hook: twelve-year-old Jesus goes missing for three days and is found asking questions
46.tomorrow: The wild man by the river
46.howItsDone: Many churches read this story in the Christmas season, and Catholics pray it as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the temple. Christian art often shows the boy seated among the teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flight into Egypt and the Holy Innocents: a family running by night. He was a refugee first.

A crowded store. A parent turns around, and the child isn't there. Now stretch that moment to three days. Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem for Passover, and this year Jesus is twelve. When the feast ends they start home with a big group of relatives and neighbors, assuming he's somewhere in the crowd. A whole day's walk later they look for him, and he's gone. They turn back. Three days of searching a packed city.
screen: `WHERE'S THE KID?` → `A WHOLE DAY'S WALK.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: They find him in the temple courts, "sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. He isn't lecturing them. He's listening, and asking, and everyone who hears him is astonished at his understanding and his answers. Then Mary speaks, in the voice of a frightened parent: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." The boy's answer is the first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" A small puzzle: the Greek is short and can be read two ways, my Father's business or my Father's house. Translators still choose between them. Either way, his first words point to God as his Father. And his parents, Luke says plainly, didn't understand. He goes home with them and is obedient to them, and Mary, again, keeps all these sayings in her heart. The four Gospels tell no other story from the years between his infancy and his adult life. Years of silence, and the one scene we're given is a boy asking questions in the house of God. Then one line for everything after: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." Even he grew, a little at a time.

segments.voice: Look for a question you've been carrying, about God, about your life, about something you were taught that never quite made sense: a real one, not a polite one. Some people hide their questions because they think faith means having answers, but the boy in this story sits in the temple asking, so say yours to yourself plainly, in one sentence. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is.

47.title: The wild man by the river (Mark 1:4–8)
47.hook: John the Baptist in camel hair calls people to turn around
47.howItsDone: Many Christians remember John the Baptist during Advent, the weeks before Christmas, when his call to prepare the way is read in church. His birth is celebrated on June 24, and in many traditions repentance is practiced through confession, private or shared, and a fresh start.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy among the doctors, listening and asking. Questions belong in the temple.

A man lives out in the wild. Rough clothes woven from camel hair, a leather belt. He eats what he can find: locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And crowds walk out of the city to hear him. Mark's Gospel doesn't open with a manger. It opens here, in the desert by the Jordan River, with this man shouting. His name is John, and people will call him John the Baptist. The whole region of Judea went out to him, Mark says, and people from Jerusalem too. What was he saying that was worth the walk?
screen: `CAMEL HAIR AND A LEATHER BELT.` → `LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY.` → `CROWDS WALK OUT TO HEAR HIM.`

segments.voice: Mark begins with the prophet Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." Then: "John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." Repentance is a heavy church word. The Greek is metanoia, built on the word for mind: a change of mind. The Hebrew prophets used a simpler word, shuv: turn around, go back. So the picture isn't mainly groveling. It's a person walking the wrong way who stops, turns, and heads home. Then John washes them in the river. Water had long been used in Jewish life for washing and becoming clean, and John makes it a sign of a fresh start. His clothes are a message too: the Bible describes the prophet Elijah the same way, hairy, with a leather belt. Then the surprise, in what John says about himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Untying sandals was a servant's job. John has crowds, fame, a following, and he spends it all pointing past himself. I baptize you with water, he says; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. His whole job is to get people turned around and facing the right way, so they'll recognize the one who's coming. The Jewish historian Josephus remembered him too, as a good man who called people to live justly.

segments.voice: Think about direction, not guilt: is there one small thing you keep walking toward that takes you somewhere you don't want to go, a habit, a tone of voice with someone, a scroll at midnight, a grudge? Name it quietly, then picture yourself stopping and turning around, not a big dramatic scene, just a turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning.
Metanoia. The Greek word for repentance, built on the word for mind: a change of mind, a turning around, the thing John called the crowds to do.
Your line: turn around. start again. Until tomorrow, when someone new walks down to John's river.

48.title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
48.hook: Jesus goes under the Jordan, and a voice says: this is my beloved son
48.howItsDone: Christians are baptized with water, usually in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: as infants in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, and as believers in Baptist and many other churches. Many churches keep the Baptism of the Lord in January, and Orthodox Christians bless water at Theophany.

segments.voice: Yesterday, metanoia: John by the river, calling crowds to change their minds and turn around.

Some words can't be earned. Nobody is called beloved because of a good report card. At the Jordan, John is baptizing crowds, people turning around and starting again. One day a man from Nazareth, about thirty years old, joins the line. He hasn't preached a sermon. He hasn't healed anyone. As far as anyone knows, he's a builder from a small town in Galilee. And John looks at him and stops.
screen: `SOME WORDS CAN'T BE EARNED.` → `A MAN FROM NAZARETH JOINS THE LINE.` → `JOHN STOPS.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse, an ordinary Greek word for putting something under. John tries to refuse: "I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?" Jesus answers: "Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness." Suffer here means allow. So he goes down into the water, like everyone else in the line. Readers have asked ever since why he would stand with people turning from their wrongs. One old answer: he chose to stand exactly where they stood. He comes up out of the water, and "the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him." And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at the timing. No miracles yet, no teaching, no followers. Beloved first; the work comes after. Christians who confess the Trinity see it here: the Father's voice, the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, in one scene. Catholics and others in the West keep a feast of the Baptism of the Lord. Orthodox Christians call it Theophany, God shown, and bless water. Baptism became the door into the church, though churches do it differently. Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Anglicans baptize babies. Baptists and others baptize those old enough to profess faith. Some pour, some sprinkle, some go all the way under. The words said over the water come from the end of Matthew's Gospel: in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

While it runs, notice that you haven't done anything to earn this moment; you're just here. If you pray, hear the word beloved as spoken to you; if not, let the water be water.
Baptism. From the Greek for dip or plunge. Washing with water as a door into a new life, and the scene where Jesus is called beloved before he does a thing.
Your line: beloved, before anything else. Tomorrow that word gets tested. See you in the desert.

49.title: Forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11)
49.hook: hungry and alone, he's offered bread, spectacle and power, and says no three times
49.howItsDone: Many churches keep Lent, the forty days before Easter, in memory of these forty days, with fasting, prayer and giving; the temptation story is often read on the first Sunday of Lent. Practices range from giving up a food or habit to fasting on set days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism: the voice that called him beloved before he'd done a thing. Beloved, before anything else. And today, the end of week seven.

Hunger changes how a person thinks. Not snack hunger. Skip two meals and everything gets louder, and judgment gets worse. Now stretch that much further. Right after the voice at the river, Matthew says, the Spirit leads Jesus up into the wilderness. He fasts forty days and forty nights. And then, with a kind of dry understatement, the text says he was hungry. That's when the tempter comes. Not at the start, when he's strong. At the end, when he's weakest.
screen: `HUNGER CHANGES THINGS.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.` → `THE TEMPTER COMES AT THE END.`

segments.voice: The first words, in the King James Bible: "If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread." If. The voice at the river just said, this is my beloved Son. The first temptation goes straight for that: prove it. The answer: "It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." Then a pinnacle of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. A spectacle. Make them believe. "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Then a high mountain, and all the kingdoms of the world, offered for one act of worship. Power, the fast way. "Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve." Bread, spectacle, power. Three refusals. And all three answers come from one book, Deuteronomy, from the chapters where Moses remembers Israel's forty years in the wilderness, when they were hungry and tested too. Forty years for a people, forty days for one man, answering with the words his people learned in the desert. Churches that keep Lent count forty days before Easter in memory of these forty, fasting a little and saying no to something. This week began in the temple with Simeon's Nunc dimittis and Anna's thanks. Then the magi, a family fleeing to Egypt, a boy asking questions, a wild man by the river, the baptism, and now the desert. Beloved first. Then tested.
screen: `IF THOU BE THE SON OF GOD.` · `BREAD, SPECTACLE, POWER.` · `THREE ANSWERS FROM DEUTERONOMY.` · `FORTY YEARS, FORTY DAYS.` · then, large: `NOT BY BREAD ALONE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small temptation that finds you on an ordinary day, not the biggest one: the extra hour on the phone, the sharp reply, the thing you buy to feel better, the shortcut. Picture the moment it usually arrives, when you're tired or hungry or bored, and picture yourself saying no to it, once, calmly. If you pray, you can ask for strength for that moment.

Temptation. Three offers of bread, spectacle and power, tested after forty days alone in the wilderness. This week's words: Nunc dimittis, the magi, the Holy Innocents, the boy among the doctors, metanoia, baptism.
Your line: not by bread alone. Next week, the road through Galilee fills up with fishermen. That's week seven.
